title: Raga Gond
hookLine: a raga where a weaver, a cloth printer and a leatherworker sing beside the Gurus

lines: A WEAVER, A PRINTER, A LEATHERWORKER.
THE SAME HEADING AS THE GURUS.
cards: A weaver. A cloth printer. A leatherworker.

That's how tradition remembers Kabir, Namdev and Ravidas: by their work, in a world where, tradition says, such work kept people far from the front of the temple. Now open the Guru Granth Sahib to the raga after Bilaval.
Their hymns are there, under the same heading as the Gurus', sung to the same raga, bowed to in the same book. Today: Raga Gond.

teach.h: NOT A SESAME SEED OF EFFORT WASTED.
teach.b: Gond opens with Guru Ram Das, and one of his first lines is worth carrying, in paraphrase: the Lord knows everything that happens inside a person, and lets not even a sesame seed's worth of anyone's effort go to waste.
Second, the Bhagats: the Sikh name for the devotional poets, not Gurus themselves, whose hymns the Gurus set beside their own.
Gond makes room for them: Kabir the weaver, Namdev, Ravidas. Third, two of their voices.

teach.h: NOTHING EQUALS SINGING THE LORD'S PRAISE.
teach.b: Namdev, in paraphrase: great sacrifices, giving away your weight in gold, bathing where the holy rivers meet at Prayag, none of these equals singing the Lord's praise.
Ravidas, in paraphrase: Mukand, Mukand, the Liberator; chant that name, world, for without the Liberator the body comes to nothing. Neither argues for his own importance.
They point past themselves, and past every ceremony, to the Name. Fourth, why it matters.

teach.h: A SCRIPTURE IS A LIST OF WHO GETS HEARD.
teach.b: A scripture is a list of who gets heard. The Gurus could have kept their book to their own line. Instead they made room for a weaver and a leatherworker, and Gond is one place you hear them.
That's why it's called the bhagats' raga here. Guru Ram Das's line reads differently now: not a sesame seed of anyone's effort wasted. Not a weaver's, either.

how: Hymns of the Bhagats, such as Kabir, Namdev and Ravidas, are sung in kirtan from the Guru Granth Sahib alongside the Gurus' hymns, and Sikhs bow to the whole Granth, Bhagat bani included, as the Guru.

o: a raga sung only by temple musicians of high caste
the raga after Bilaval, where Bhagats sing beside the Gurus
a raga of village dances sung at harvest time

games.q: you're compiling a scripture. a weaver and a leatherworker have sung beautiful hymns to the One. what do you do?
o: keep the book to the Gurus' own line.
set their hymns beside the Gurus', under the same ragas.
put them in a separate appendix at the back.
games.why: the Gurus set the Bhagats' hymns in the Granth under the same raga headings, and Gond is one place you hear them.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose work you rely on and rarely notice: the person who cleans the building, drives the bus, picks the fruit, answers the phone.
Hold their face, or imagine one, and let their effort count, not one sesame seed of it wasted, with one Waheguru for them if you pray, or simply keeping them in mind if you don't.
